title: Travel in China
intro: Getting around mainland China: greetings, help, transport, hotels, food, paying and emergencies.

scenes.title: Greetings and politeness basics
scenes.description: What a traveller says all day: hello to one person, to a group and politely; thank you and the replies; sorry vs excuse me (对不起 / 不好意思 / 打扰一下 / 请问); goodbye; short yes/no-type answers; declining an offer; plus the formulas shop and restaurant staff say to you.

phrases.english: Hello! / Hi!
phrases.usage: The all-purpose greeting to one person (HSK level 1). Official listening items use it as a greeting (女：你好！ 男：你好！很高兴认识你。) and, very usefully for travellers, as the polite attention-getter before a request to shop staff, a cashier or a taxi driver: 你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我去世界公园。 / 你好，一共多少钱？ You will hear 你好 or 您好 back. For older people or formal situations use 您好 (see below). With friends, family and people you see every day 你好 sounds stiff — greet them by name or title, with 早 in the morning, or casually (see the rule on greeting people you know).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Thank you! / Thanks!
phrases.usage: Standard thanks (HSK level 1). Add a pronoun for warmth or respect: 谢谢你 / 谢谢您 (polite) / 谢谢你们 (to several people). The usual reply you will hear is 不客气. The second syllable is neutral tone in the dictionary form (xièxie).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: You're welcome.
phrases.usage: The standard reply to 谢谢 (HSK level 1): 男：谢谢你们！ 女：不客气。再见。 / 男：谢谢！麻烦你们了。 女：不客气。 Dictionary alternatives with the same job: 别客气 'don't mention it; no formalities, please', 不用谢 'You're welcome', 应该的 '(polite response) you're welcome; just doing my duty' (all CC-CEDICT). Pronunciation: 不 is bù in citation form but is said bú before the fourth tone of 客 — that is why the HSK syllabus prints 'bú kèqi'.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: I'm sorry.
phrases.usage: A real apology when you did something wrong or caused trouble. 现汉: '对人有愧，常用为表示抱歉的套语' (feeling one has wronged someone; the usual formula of apology), e.g. 对不起，让您久等了 'sorry to keep you waiting'. The normal reply is 没关系 (paired exactly so in the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample). Staff also use it when refusing: 先生，对不起，我们这儿不能抽烟。 For small everyday slips 不好意思 is the lighter choice (see rule).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: That's OK. / It doesn't matter.
phrases.usage: The reply to 对不起 or 不好意思. Also accepts a small problem: 男：好吧，没关系。 (after hearing no window seat is left). 没事 / 没事儿 is also heard in reassurance: 没事，不用担心 'it's nothing, don't worry'.

phrases.english: Sorry. / Excuse me. (for a small inconvenience)
phrases.usage: Light apology for small slips or for troubling someone: 甲：你的词典呢？ 乙：不好意思，我没拿来。 / 不好意思，我忘记拿词典了，下星期一还你行吗？ / 真不好意思，初次见面我就迟到了，让你久等了。 It is also the everyday “excuse me” before a request (不好意思，我迷路了。 “Excuse me, I’m lost.”), and staff use it when they can’t help (不好意思，这里不能地铁直达。 “Sorry, the metro doesn’t go there directly.”). In native-speaker service dialogues it is about four times as frequent as 对不起. CC-CEDICT lists “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” next to “to feel embarrassed” (the 5th-edition 现汉 text available here gives only the “embarrassed / too shy to” senses). HSK 2025: level 2.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Excuse me. (sorry to bother you)
phrases.usage: Say it to approach a stranger or interrupt someone; in the official examples it is followed by 请问 and the question: 打扰一下，请问，地铁站离这儿远吗？ / 打扰一下，请问在哪儿买票？ The current HSK 3.0 level-4 sample uses it to interrupt students: 打扰一下，同学，请不要在自习室里大声讨论。 When you leave after taking someone's time you can say 打扰了 ('sorry to have bothered you', CC-CEDICT), as in 好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Excuse me, what time is it?
phrases.usage: 请问 'may I ask' is the polite opener for any question to a stranger (现汉: 敬辞，用于请求对方回答问题; CC-CEDICT: 'Excuse me, may I ask...?'). Put it right before the question: 请问，这个电视多少钱？ / 请问洗手间在哪儿？ It can follow 你好/您好 or 打扰一下. This exact question is the example item of both the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample paper and the 2025 new-HSK samples.

phrases.english: Hello! (polite)
phrases.usage: Polite hello with the respectful 'you' 您 (现汉: 你/你们 '含敬意', with respect). In official dialogues it is what service staff say to customers (您好，请问您去哪儿？ — taxi driver; 先生，您好，您要办理什么业务？ — bank clerk; 您好！欢迎光临。 — restaurant). Use it yourself with older people, in formal settings, or to be extra polite before a favour: 您好！您能帮我们照张相吗？
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: 您 is routine in Beijing and the north; many southern speakers, whose home dialects have no 你/您 distinction, use it less among themselves (forum reports, anecdotal). 您好 from service staff is normal everywhere, and using 您 to older people — for example a partner’s parents — is polite in any region.

phrases.english: Thank you! (polite)

phrases.english: No thanks. (no need)
phrases.usage: Polite refusal of an offer: 女：吃点儿蛋糕吧？很好吃。 男：不用了，谢谢。 Add a reason to soften it: 不用了，我自己打车就行，谢谢你。 (“No need — I’ll just take a taxi, thank you”) / 不用了，谢谢您，我自己能行。 现汉: 不用 = “表示事实上没有必要” (there is no need). It is also the friendly way to wave off a street seller or tout; if someone keeps pushing, the firmer 不要，谢谢 (next phrase) is normal. To a shop assistant who comes over you can say 我只是看看 (“I’m just looking”).
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Good morning!
phrases.usage: Morning greeting (CC-CEDICT). 现汉 also lists plain 早 as the greeting used when people meet in the morning (“问候的话，用于早晨见面时互相招呼：老师～！”). 早安 also means “good morning”, but in the mainland it is mostly written (good-morning messages on WeChat and social media) and more usual in Taiwan; said aloud it can sound a little formal or literary, so 早 or 早上好 are the safe spoken choices. In the evening: 晚上好 “Good evening!” (CC-CEDICT); 晚安 is for parting at night (“客套话，用于晚上道别”, 现汉).
phrases.speaker: either

rules.rule: The level-1 politeness core is 你好 / 谢谢 / 对不起 / 再见, with the replies 不客气 (to thanks) and 没关系 (to an apology). Learners are expected to recognise and exchange these in meeting, parting and everyday situations.
rules.why: The 2025 HSK task syllabus (in force 2026-07) lists exchanging exactly these as a level-1 communicative task; the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample tests the 对不起 → 没关系 and 谢谢 → 不客气 pairs.

rules.rule: 您 is the respectful 'you'. Service staff address customers with 您 / 您好 (您好，请问您去哪儿？ / 您稍等). Use 您 yourself with older people, people you want to show respect to, and in formal situations. In the official dialogues customers address shop staff, clerks and drivers with 你好 + their request (你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我想办一张信用卡。 / 你好，一共多少钱？).
rules.why: 现汉 defines 您 as 你/你们 with respect ('含敬意'); the official HSK dialogues consistently show staff using 您 and customers opening with 你好.
rules.regional_note: Forum reports (anecdotal) say 您 is used routinely in Beijing, even between colleagues, while many southern speakers — whose home dialects, such as Shanghainese, have no 你/您 distinction — use it less in everyday Mandarin. Service staff say 您 everywhere, and 您 to older people (for example a partner’s parents) is polite in any region.

rules.rule: Addressing people you don't know: get staff's attention with 你好 or, in restaurants and hotels, 服务员 (服务员，请给我来一杯咖啡。 / 服务员，我们想再要一个菜。). Call a taxi driver or any skilled worker (a cook 厨师傅, a carpenter 木匠师傅) 师傅 (师傅，我去火车站。); 师傅 also follows a surname (王师傅). Staff will call you 先生 'sir' or 女士 'madam' (both HSK level 1). Students are addressed as 同学 (同学，请问图书馆怎么走？ / 打扰一下，同学，……).
rules.why: 现汉: 师傅 = '对有技艺的人的尊称' (respectful title for someone with a skill/trade), 服务员 = staff who serve guests in hotels, restaurants etc.; CC-CEDICT adds 'respectful form of address for older men' for 师傅. The forms are shown in use in official HSK/YCT dialogues.

rules.rule: In mainland China do not call a waitress or shop assistant 小姐 on its own: the word picked up the slang sense “sex worker”, and the older textbooks that taught it are out of date. Use 服务员 or 你好 instead (美女 / 帅哥 in casual places — see the next rule). Surname + 小姐 (王小姐 “Ms Wang”) is still fine in formal and business settings, and 女士 is the safe formal “madam”. In Taiwan and Hong Kong 小姐 for staff is still normal.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT records the slang sense “(slang) prostitute” for 小姐. The 2009-2010 Hanban HSK papers still had customers call female staff 小姐 (小姐，请问表演什么时候开始？ / 小姐，你好，你这儿有杯子吗？); the national 2021 standard listed 小姐 at level 1, but the 2025 HSK syllabus moved it to level 5, and none of the HSK 3.0 / 2025 sample items examined uses it as a call to staff. Current teaching sources (Kaiwa 2026, italki, Digmandarin, Chinese-forums) agree that bare 小姐 is avoided for staff in the mainland while 王小姐-style name + 小姐 remains usable.
rules.regional_note: Teaching sources say the negative connotation is felt most strongly in northern cities such as Beijing and Harbin and less in the south — but avoiding bare 小姐 for staff is the safe choice everywhere in the mainland.

rules.rule: 美女 (“beautiful woman”) and 帅哥 (“handsome guy”) are widely used as casual forms of address, especially to call young staff in shops and restaurants. They are informal, and some people find them a bit tacky (土) or uncomfortable, so with older people or in formal places stick to 你好, 服务员, 师傅 and 先生 / 女士.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT lists “handsome (form of address)” under 帅哥; the dictionaries do not record the address use of 美女, but magazine and teaching sources do: The World of Chinese (2018) says both are still used in the service industry (popular from the mid-2000s to the early 2010s, with a somewhat working-class flavour); Digmandarin calls them relaxed address terms between peers; a Kunming forum thread reports 美女 / 帅哥 as the local way to call waiting staff, with some finding it “uncouth” and younger educated speakers preferring 服务员; a 2026 teaching blog recommends 美女 for staff only in casual places.

rules.rule: Choose the “sorry / excuse me” word by situation: 对不起 = apology when you have wronged or troubled someone (reply 没关系); 不好意思 = lighter “sorry” for small slips and inconveniences, and the everyday “excuse me” before a request; 抱歉 = “sorry”, used e.g. by staff and in announcements (抱歉，先生，这里禁止吸烟。 / 我们很抱歉地通知您……); 打扰一下 = “excuse me” when approaching or interrupting someone; 请问 = “may I ask”, placed directly before a question. Sequence attested for approaching strangers: 打扰一下，请问，… ？ In Beijing you may also hear 劳驾 (“excuse me / may I trouble you”, also to get past people); it is northern and rather old-fashioned, so use 请问, 不好意思 or 打扰一下 yourself — especially in the south.
rules.why: 现汉 defines 对不起 as the apology formula for having wronged someone and 请问 as an honorific for asking someone to answer a question; CC-CEDICT gives 不好意思 “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” and 打扰了 “sorry to interrupt you”; the official dialogues show each word in these roles. On 劳驾: teaching and dictionary sites (HanyuGuide, FluentU, That’s Mandarin) describe it as northern and old-fashioned, the 2025 HSK syllabus places it at levels 7-9, and native-speaker dialogue corpora use 请问 about 700 times as often.

rules.rule: Spoken morning greeting: 早 or 早上好. 早安 also means “good morning”, but in the mainland it is mostly written (good-morning messages on WeChat and social media) and more usual in Taiwan; said aloud it can sound a little formal or literary. 晚安 means “good night” when parting, not “good evening” as a greeting (that is 晚上好).
rules.why: 现汉 entries 早 (sense ❺), 早安 (“多见于翻译作品” in the 5th-edition text) and 晚安 (“用于晚上道别”); CC-CEDICT 晚上好 “Good evening!”; the 新华 词语 data defines 早安 as a greeting formula (“套语。用于早晨见面时互相问候”); teaching sites (Migaku, Preply) describe 早上好 as the mainland standard and 早安 as typical of Taiwan and written messages.

rules.rule: 你好 is for strangers, service staff and first meetings. With friends, family and people you see every day it sounds stiff and formal. Greet them instead by name or title (老师好 to a teacher), with 早 in the morning, with a casual 嗨 / 哈喽 (common among younger people), with a small question about their day (吃了吗？ “have you eaten?”, 去哪儿？ “where are you off to?”), or with 好久不见 when you haven’t met for a while.
rules.why: Teaching sites (LTL, Hack Chinese, New Concept Mandarin, an Everyday Chinese course) describe 你好 as formal, used mainly when meeting someone new and not normally among friends, and list these alternatives; native-speaker dialogue writers open casually with 哈喽 / 嗨 as well as 你好.

scenes.title: When you don't understand
scenes.description: Signalling that you didn't hear or didn't understand, asking for a repeat, checking meaning and pronunciation, saying how much Chinese you speak, asking for English, and asking someone to wait.

phrases.english: I didn't understand (what you said).
phrases.usage: Say it when you heard the words but didn't understand them: 男：天“短”了是什么意思？我没听懂。 / 女：对不起，我没听懂，您说得太快了。 没听懂 = didn't catch/understand this time. For a general inability (e.g. a strong accent or dialect) the dictionary form is 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing' (CC-CEDICT), as in the national standard's example 刚来中国时，他一句中文也听不懂。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.pinyin: Nǐ shuō shénme? Wǒ méi tīngjiàn.
phrases.pinyin_as_source: Nǐ shuō shénme ？ Wǒ méi tīngjiàn ．
phrases.literal: you say what? I not hear-perceive
phrases.english: What did you say? I didn't hear (you).
phrases.usage: For when you literally didn’t hear (noise, a bad phone line). 没听见 = didn’t hear; 没听懂 = heard but didn’t understand. On the phone: 女：喂？你听见我说话了吗？ 男：你说什么？你再说一次？ With a stranger a softer opener is 不好意思，我没听清楚 (“sorry, I didn’t catch that”) — 现汉’s example: 你刚才说的话我没听清楚，你从起头儿再说一遍。
phrases.speaker: me

verification.notes: Checker OK and grammatical, but the register was wrong: 再说一次吧 is a casual suggestion between people who know each other (the YCT source is a conversation between acquaintances), not the polite request a traveller needs. In the independent native-speaker data 再说一遍 is the usual collocation (CrossWOZ+RiSAWOZ: 再说一遍 8, 再说一次 0; Tatoeba: 10 vs 0), so the polite forms 请再说一遍 and 不好意思，能再说一遍吗？ were added as new phrases. Previous values — old register: “neutral” | old english: “Say it once more, please.” | old usage: “Ask someone to repeat; 吧 makes it a soft request. In the source a woman who lost her phone asks for a number again: 以前有，我的电话丢了，再说一次吧。 On a bad line: 你说什么？你再说一次？ A politer frame from another HSK dialogue is 麻烦您再发一遍吧 ('could you please send it again'); 遍 counts one complete run-through (现汉). The textbook sentence 请再说一遍 was not found in the sources seen (see open_questions).”.

phrases.english: Do you speak English?
phrases.usage: SLOT CHANGED: the source sentence is 你会说汉语吗？ ('Do you speak Chinese?'); only the language name was replaced (汉语 → 英语). 英文 is also used for 'English' (CC-CEDICT gives both 英语 and 英文 as 'English (language)'; national standard example: 除了英文，他还会说中文。). Split check: 「我不会说」 Wǒ bù huì shuō = ok, 「中文。」 Zhōngwén. = ok”.

phrases.english: Slower, please! / Slow down!
phrases.usage: Said to someone going too fast — in the source to a driver: 你开得太快了！慢一点儿！ (also 你还是开慢点儿吧 “you’d better drive slower”). 现汉 shows the same pattern after a verb: 你走慢一点儿 (“walk a bit slower”). For speech, put 说 in front: 请说慢一点 (see that phrase).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Southern speakers usually drop the -r: 慢一点.

rules.rule: Pick the verb for what went wrong: 没听见 = I didn’t hear it; 没听懂 = I heard it but didn’t understand; 听不懂 = I can’t understand (the speech/language — also a dialect: 我听不懂粤语 “I can’t understand Cantonese”); 看不懂 = I can’t make sense of something written or seen (sign, map, menu); 不明白 = I don’t understand the meaning or the point.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 听见 'to hear', 听懂 'to understand (on hearing)', 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing', 看不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is looking at'; 现汉 明白 ❹ '知道；了解'. Official items use them exactly so (你说什么？我没听见。 / 我没听懂 / 这张地图我看不懂 / 有个句子的意思我不明白).

scenes.title: Asking for help and directions
scenes.description: Asking where something is and how to get there, whether it is far, finding the toilet or a metro station, saying you are lost, asking a stranger for a favour — and the typical answers you will hear (go straight, turn left/right, opposite, right ahead, not far).

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
phrases.usage: Pattern 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ Official exchange: 男：请问洗手间在哪儿？ 女：您向前走，左边就是。 Also attested with 哪里: 请问，男洗手间在哪里？ ('Where is the men's toilet?'). 洗手间 is the polite word (现汉: 婉辞，指厕所). Swap the place (slot): 地铁站 metro station, 出口 exit, 二零四房间 room 204 (请问，二零四房间在哪儿？).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Speakers from the south usually say 哪里 (请问洗手间在哪里？); 哪儿 with the -r ending is typical of Beijing and the north. Both are standard and understood everywhere.

verification.notes: check.mjs (and the ingest checker scripts/lib/cedict.mjs, same algorithm) FAILs this item: forward maximum matching takes 到了 as the CC-CEDICT word 到了 [dao4 liao3] “at last; finally”. Here it is the verb 到 dào + the particle 了 le (CC-CEDICT 了 [le5]); the split check passes. The pinyin is correct and must not be changed to dào liǎo. Content verified, but status is left “unverified” because the rule is “verified only when the checker passes”; rewording to dodge the tool (dropping 了) would lose the most natural form, so the lead should either add a split fallback to the checker or accept this item manually. Independent sources: distance + direction answers in native-speaker data and Tatoeba. Previous values — old check: “warn: check.mjs reports FAIL (到了: mismatch (given dào le; CC-CEDICT dào liǎo)) — resolved as false positive: the segmenter takes 到了 as the CC-CEDICT word 到了 [dao4 liao3] 'at last; finally'; here it is 到 dào + the particle 了 le (CC-CEDICT 了 [le5]). Split check: 「你往前走一百米就到」 = ok, 「了。」 le. = ok”.

verification.notes: check.mjs (and the ingest checker scripts/lib/cedict.mjs, same algorithm) FAILs this item: forward maximum matching takes 到了 as the CC-CEDICT word 到了 [dao4 liao3] “at last; finally”. Here it is the verb 到 dào + the particle 了 le (CC-CEDICT 了 [le5]); the split check passes. The pinyin is correct and must not be changed to dào liǎo. Content verified, but status is left “unverified” because the rule is “verified only when the checker passes”; rewording to dodge the tool (dropping 了) would lose the most natural form, so the lead should either add a split fallback to the checker or accept this item manually. Independent sources: another YCT paper has 就在前面，很近 as the answer to “is the station far?”, and a native-speaker dialogue uses 不远，走路就过去了. Previous values — old check: “warn: check.mjs reports FAIL (到了: mismatch (given dào le; CC-CEDICT dào liǎo)) — resolved as false positive: the segmenter takes 到了 as the CC-CEDICT word 到了 [dao4 liao3] 'at last; finally'; here it is 到 dào + the particle 了 le (CC-CEDICT 了 [le5]). Split check: 「不远，就在前面，再走五分钟就到」 = ok, 「了。」 le. = ok”.

phrases.hanzi: 你再向南走两百米就能看到了。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ zài xiàng nán zǒu liǎngbǎi mǐ jiù néng kàndào le.
phrases.literal: you further toward south walk two-hundred metre then can see (particle)
phrases.english: Walk another 200 metres south and you'll see it.
phrases.usage: Directions may use compass points (东 east, 南 south, 西 west, 北 north) instead of left/right. Other official answers: 就在路东 ('on the east side of the road'), 就在超市西边 ('just west of the supermarket'), 北门左边 ('left of the north gate'). Here the asker had said 我现在就在学校西门 ('I'm at the school's west gate').
phrases.speaker: them
phrases.regional_note: Teaching sources say compass directions are typical of northern cities with grid-plan streets (e.g. Beijing), while in southern cities, with rivers and hills, people more often say left/right (and up/down). This is a widely repeated impression rather than a studied rule — in the south be ready for both.

phrases.hanzi: 劳驾，去中国银行怎么走？
phrases.pinyin: Láojià, qù Zhōngguó Yínháng zěnme zǒu?
phrases.english: Excuse me, how do I get to the Bank of China?
phrases.usage: 劳驾 'excuse me / may I trouble you' — 现汉: 客套话，用于请别人做事或让路 (polite phrase for asking someone to do something or to make way), e.g. 劳驾，请让让路。 ('Excuse me, please let me through'). Answer in the source: 前面路口往右拐就是。 Note: the 2025 HSK syllabus lists 劳驾 only at levels 7-9, while 请问 is level 1, and the newer (2021-2025) sample items examined use 请问 and 打扰一下 instead. Swap the destination (slot).
phrases.speaker: me

verification.notes: Not wrong Chinese, but the wrong phrase to teach this learner as something to say: 劳驾 is northern (Beijing) and rather old-fashioned. rules.rule: Asking the way: [打扰一下，] 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ / 去 + place + 怎么走？ / 附近有 + place + 吗？ / place + 离这儿远吗？ Thank with 谢谢 or 好的，谢谢. Asking the way and understanding simple directions (direction, position, route, time) is an HSK level-1/level-2 task.
rules.why: All four question frames occur in official HSK/YCT dialogues; the 2025 HSK task syllabus lists 问路 (asking the way) and understanding 指路 (directions: 行进方向、位置、路线、时长、乘车信息) at levels 1-2.

rules.rule: Be ready for compass points in directions: 东 (east), 南 (south), 西 (west), 北 (north) — e.g. 向南走两百米, 就在路东, 就在超市西边, 北门左边.
rules.why: Several official answers give directions this way instead of (or together with) left/right.
rules.regional_note: Teaching sources say compass directions are typical of northern cities with grid-plan streets (e.g. Beijing), while in southern cities people more often use left/right (and up/down). This is a widely repeated impression rather than a studied rule — be ready for both.

rules.rule: Three words for 'toilet': 洗手间 = the polite euphemism (the polite choice when asking); 卫生间 = a room with sanitary fittings, i.e. the bathroom/toilet of a flat or hotel, also a toilet in general; 厕所 = the general, non-euphemistic word. HSK 2025 levels: 洗手间 2, 卫生间 3, 厕所 4.
rules.why: 现汉: 洗手间 '婉辞，指厕所'; 卫生间 '旅馆、住宅等处有卫生设备的房间；厕所'; 厕所 '专供人大小便的地方'. Levels from the 2025 HSK vocabulary syllabus.

rules.rule: 哪儿 and 哪里 both mean 'where' and are both HSK level-1 words; 现汉 labels 哪儿 as colloquial (〈口〉) and defines it as 哪里. Official dialogues use both for the same question (请问洗手间在哪儿？ / 请问，男洗手间在哪里？). The same pairing exists for 这儿/这里 'here' and 那儿/那里 'there'.
rules.why: 2025 HSK vocabulary syllabus (哪里 nǎlǐ, 哪儿 nǎr, level 1); 现汉 entries 哪儿 and 那儿 (〈口〉).
rules.regional_note: The -r (儿化) forms 哪儿 / 这儿 / 那儿 / 一点儿 are typical of Beijing and northern speech; southern speakers usually avoid them and say 哪里, 这里, 那里 and 一点 (some Southwestern Mandarin areas such as Chengdu and Chongqing do use -r). From a south/central-China family you are likely to hear 哪里 / 这里 / 一点 more often; both sets are standard. In native-speaker dialogue corpora 哪里 outnumbers 哪儿 about 8 to 1, and 这里 outnumbers 这儿 about 9 to 1.

scenes.description: Getting into a taxi or ride-hailing car, giving the destination, phone calls with the driver or the person picking you up, stopping, paying, receipts and lost items. rules.rule: Address taxi drivers as 师傅 (shīfu): 师傅，我去火车站。 Bus drivers are also called 师傅 (问问师傅在哪儿下 "ask the driver where to get off").
rules.why: 师傅 is the respectful term for skilled workers and drivers (CC-CEDICT: 'master; qualified worker; respectful form of address for older men'). The HSK 4 sample uses it for a taxi driver, and native-written RiSAWOZ dialogues (2020) use it for bus drivers.

rules.rule: Ask for the taxi receipt (跟司机要发票) and keep it: it carries the taxi company's phone number, which is how you trace something left in the car.
rules.why: In the HSK 5 sample the friend of someone who left a bag in a taxi asks first about the receipt, because 发票上有出租车公司的电话; in an HSK 3 reading a traveller who left a suitcase in a taxi expects to find it because 我有出租车票. Dated practical detail: both are HSK 2.0-era sample papers; whether receipts are now mainly paper or electronic, and how ride-hailing apps handle lost items, was not verified this session.

rules.rule: Where to sit in a five-seat car: when the host drives you personally (a relative or colleague taking you out), the front passenger seat is the polite seat for the guest; in official/business reception with a driver, the seat behind the front passenger is the most polite seat, and the front passenger seat (随员座) is for an interpreter or secretary, so putting a guest there is impolite. For safety, the rear middle seat is safest, and everyone should wear a seat belt (系上安全带).
rules.why: HSK 6 sample reading 81-84 (citing experts): "在社交应酬中，如果是主人自驾车陪客人出去游玩，那么副驾驶座就是最有礼貌的座位。而在公务接待中，副驾驶座后面的座位是最礼貌的座位。公务接待时，副驾驶座被称为“随员座”，一般是翻译、秘书的位置，让客人坐在这里是不礼貌的。" Relevant when family or business contacts pick you up.

rules.rule: Taxi vocabulary: 出租车 (taxi), 打车 (take a taxi), 叫车 (call a cab / request a ride in an app), 网约车 (app-based car), 滴滴 (DiDi). CC-CEDICT also lists 打的 dǎdī (colloquial 'take a taxi') and 的士 dīshì (loanword 'taxi'), and notes that in Taiwan 出租车 can mean 'rental car'.
rules.why: Knowing which word means what avoids confusion when ordering a ride or reading an app.
rules.regional_note: CC-CEDICT marks the Taiwan meaning of 出租车 ('rental car'); no mainland north/south difference in these words was verified this session.

rules.rule: Expect to pay by phone: a business-Chinese (BCT) sample text published by CLEC says mobile payment has become a new way of paying and many people no longer carry cash or credit cards when they go out; the new HSK syllabus (2025) uses 坐高铁出行，用手机支付 as examples of everyday modern life, and 扫码 ('scan a QR code') is an HSK word. Card acceptance is not guaranteed (an HSK 5 sample shop answers 我们这里只能用现金付款 'we only take cash').
rules.why: Paying is the last step of every taxi ride and hotel stay. How foreign visitors link foreign bank cards to Alipay or WeChat Pay was not verified this session (see open_questions).

scenes.title: Trains: tickets, seats and the station
scenes.description: Buying a train ticket at a counter (date, destination, number, seat class, window seat), departure and arrival times, finding your way in the station, seats on board, delays and changes, and what staff and announcements say. Official rail procedures for foreign passports could not be verified this session (see open_questions).

rules.rule: High-speed train seats (高铁/动车) are sold by class: 二等座 (second class, the cheaper standard choice) and 一等座 (first class); the seller asks 您想要一等座还是二等座？ CC-CEDICT also lists the classes of conventional trains: 硬座 (hard seat), 硬卧 (hard sleeper), 软卧 (soft sleeper).
rules.why: In the RiSAWOZ train dialogues the agent offers exactly these two classes and 二等座 is the cheaper one in the examples seen (e.g. 二等座134.5元 vs 一等座229.5元 for one Shanghai–Nanjing train in the 2020 dataset; illustrative, not current fares).

rules.rule: On the metro and buses, when you hear 下一站就要到了，请下车的乘客提前做好准备, move to the door before your stop.

rules.rule: Hotel check-in follows a fixed pattern: you say what you booked and your surname (我前天订了一个标准间，我姓王); reception looks it up (您稍等，我查一下), asks for an ID document (请出示一下您的身份证) and does the check-in formalities (办理入住手续), then hands over the key card (这是您的房卡，请拿好).
rules.why: Knowing the steps makes the exchange predictable. For foreign guests the ID document is the passport; current police-registration rules for foreigners, and whether every hotel may accept foreign guests, were not verified this session (see open_questions).

rules.rule: 标准间 is a standard two-person room (CC-CEDICT: 'two-person room of standard size and amenities'), 大床房 has one double/queen/king bed, and 单人间 is a single room. Booking staff ask 您想要大床房还是标准间？
rules.why: Couples and colleagues need different room types; the words are easy to confuse.

rules.rule: When you ring or approach staff about a problem, give your room number first (我住六零七 / 我住八零七), then what is wrong (……坏了), then the request (你能来看看吗？). Room numbers are read digit by digit, with 零 for zero.
rules.why: Two HSK sample dialogues with hotel staff follow exactly this order (我住六零七……空调坏了……你能来看看吗？ and 我住八零七……还有早饭吗？), which lets staff act at once.

rules.rule: To get a staff member's attention, start with 你好/您好 (as guests do in several of these sample dialogues) or say 服务员 ('attendant'). Avoid 小姐 for female staff even though HSK 2.0-era sample papers still use it (e.g. 小姐，我女儿多少钱一张票？), because CC-CEDICT records the slang meaning 'prostitute'.
rules.why: 小姐 is ambiguous; 你好 and 服务员 are neutral. A native-teacher source explicitly describing 小姐 as dated for service staff could not be consulted this session (see open_questions).
